claims.claim: The Quill to Live book club reports that half the group scored Tigana nine or above and the other half scored it below five, for an average of a solid seven.
claims.source: Andrew, 'Book Club Discussion: Tigana By Guy Gavriel Kay', The Quill to Live, 17 March 2016
claims.quote: half of the group had scores of nine or above

claims.claim: The Quill to Live book club reports that some readers found the pacing jarring because the perspective often jumps from point of view to point of view.
claims.source: Andrew reporting the anti-Tigana camp, The Quill to Live, 17 March 2016
claims.quote: the perspective often jumps from point-of-view to point-of-view

claims.claim: The Quill to Live book club reports that some readers found Kay's writing pretentious and said they preferred more austere prose.
claims.source: Andrew reporting the anti-Tigana camp, The Quill to Live, 17 March 2016
claims.quote: found the writing pretentious and that they preferred more austere prose

claims.claim: The forum member Erfael says there are no extras in Kay's books: the stories concern how each character's presence affects history at a given point or how history affects them.
claims.source: Erfael, in the thread 'Question regarding Guy Gavriel Kay's books', SFFWorld forum, 6 December 2011
claims.quote: how history affects them at a given point

claims.claim: Erfael says Kay works in a style where everything that happens is somehow important or represented, which can come across as contrived.
claims.quote: everything that happens is somehow important or represented

claims.claim: The thread's opening poster says Tigana is almost written like a play, being long conversations of pure dialogue with little else.
claims.quote: The book is almost written like a play.

claims.claim: The forum member chokipokilo says Kay uses flashbacks and internal monologues a great deal and that the way he blends history into the narrative amazes him.
claims.quote: The way he blends history into the narrative

claims.claim: chokipokilo says the coincidental revelation is a device Kay uses in all his works and that after a few books a reader starts to see it coming.
claims.quote: that's a device GGK uses in all his works

claims.claim: The forum member Severn reports lovely, subtle differences in Kay's tone and manner of writing between Tigana and The Last Light of the Sun.
claims.quote: subtle differences in his tone and manner of writing

claims.claim: The reviewer at Tar Vol On describes The Lions of Al-Rassan as told in an old-school third-person omniscient narration that mostly follows three characters.
claims.source: tarvolon, 'Fantasy Novel Review: The Lions of Al-Rassan by Guy Gavriel Kay', Tar Vol On, 4 February 2021
claims.quote: an old school, third-person omniscient narration

claims.feature: other: the inevitable left off the page
claims.claim: Katherine Olley says that once events become inevitable Kay largely leaves them to be supplied by the imagination of the reader.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, 'Guy Gavriel Kay: A Short Introduction', University of Oxford Podcasts video lecture, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: he largely leaves them to be supplied by the imagination

claims.claim: Olley says almost the entire An Lushan rebellion in Under Heaven - its years of upheaval, victories, losses, alliances and political manoeuvrings - is condensed into an epilogue.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: all of that is condensed into an epilogue

claims.claim: Olley says that rather than building suspense Kay encourages reflection, looking back with the tragic clarity of hindsight rather than forward with bated breath.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: to look back with the tragic clarity of hindsight

claims.claim: Olley names the retrospective construction of history and its many ironies as one of Kay's chief thematic concerns across all his works.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: The nature of history is retrospective construction

claims.claim: Olley says Kay shows little interest in hitting the predictable beats of a historical period, focusing instead on the smaller, more personal moments behind the scenes that shape larger events.
claims.source: Katherine Olley, University of Oxford Podcasts, 16 December 2020
claims.quote: little interest in hitting the predictable beats of the historical period
